pages.text: Stand in an open market at midday. Your eyes see bright light. Your skin feels warmth. A few hours later, your skin may be sore, although you felt nothing strike it. Three different things reached you from the Sun at once: light that you can see, infrared rays that you can feel as heat, and ultraviolet rays that you can neither see nor feel. They all belong to one family, called the electromagnetic spectrum. Most of the family is invisible. Its members cook food, carry phone calls, show broken bones, and treat cancer. Some can also harm us.

pages.text: All electromagnetic waves can cross empty space, and there they all travel at the speed of light. What differs is the wavelength. Radio waves are the longest: some are longer than a football pitch. Then, in order, come microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays, and gamma rays, whose wavelengths are smaller than an atom. As the wavelength gets shorter, the frequency gets higher, and each wave carries more energy. Our eyes detect only the narrow band in the middle. The colours of a rainbow, from red to violet, are simply the different wavelengths of visible light.

pages.text: The long, low-energy waves are our messengers. Radio waves carry radio and television programmes across the country. Microwaves carry mobile phone calls and Wi-Fi, and inside a microwave oven they make the water in food vibrate and heat up. Infrared rays leave every warm object. A television remote control sends its signals by infrared, and some thermometers read your temperature from the infrared your forehead gives out. None of these waves has enough energy to break apart the atoms in your body. If they are strong, their main effect is gentle heating.

pages.text: Ultraviolet rays carry more energy. A little is useful: it helps the skin to make vitamin D, and ultraviolet lamps kill germs in water and on hospital tools. Too much burns the skin, damages the eyes, and, over many years, can lead to skin cancer. Dark skin contains more melanin, a natural substance that absorbs ultraviolet, but it does not give complete protection. People with albinism have very little melanin and must take special care. Shade, long sleeves, a wide hat, and sunglasses all help. High in the atmosphere, a layer of ozone gas absorbs most of the Sun’s ultraviolet before it reaches us.

pages.text: X-rays and gamma rays carry the most energy of all. X-rays pass through flesh but are stopped by bone, so they make shadow pictures of a broken arm or a damaged chest. Gamma rays come from radioactive materials. These rays can damage living cells, which makes them dangerous, but the same power is used in radiotherapy, where carefully aimed beams destroy cancer cells. Ghana’s large teaching hospitals, such as Korle Bu in Accra and Komfo Anokye in Kumasi, offer this treatment. The person who takes your X-ray stands behind a screen, because a small dose for you would become a large dose for someone exposed all day.

pages.text: Invisible rays also bring news from space. At Kuntunse, near Accra, stands a dish 32 metres wide. It was built to carry telephone signals by satellite, and in 2017 it began a new life as a radio telescope, the first of its kind in West Africa. It collects radio waves from far-off objects such as pulsars. A pulsar is the tiny, heavy remains of an exploded star. It spins many times a second and sweeps a beam of radio waves past Earth like a lighthouse. So are these rays friends or enemies? Neither. Each must be understood, used wisely, and respected.
